s: The breastworks and battlements before the Achaean wall are fiercely contested by Lycians, Argives, and Danaans. During the assault, Sarpedon tears away a battlement to open a breach; Trojans and allies overthrow the defenses and pull up their buttresses, before Hector springs toward them and breaks through the gates.
The doors at the gates are double and high, secured by two cross-bars and one key; Hector's blow breaks both hinges, defeats the bars, and flings them open in opposite directions.
A large stone outside the gates, thick at one end and pointed at the other, is lifted by Hector and breaks the hinges, opening the gates.

l: the breaking of the gates, The Iliad
s: The breaking of the gates occurs when Hector strikes their double doors with a great stone. The hinges break, the cross-bars no longer hold, and the doors fly open, allowing Hector and the Trojans to enter.

is_led_by Hector son of Priam [at the Achaean ships] Hector’s force advances in a dense body toward the Achaean ships and initially appears capable of overrunning the tents and fleet. The force is halted by the closely packed Achaean battalions, though Hector urges the Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanians to stand firm.

This is a battle and close combat between the Achaeans, Argives, Danaans, and Trojans, centered on the ships after the Trojans break through the wall and gates. It matters because both sides see its outcome as deciding whether the Achaeans survive or the Trojans burn the fleet. It begins as fierce close-quarters fighting, with dense formations and spears, swords, bows, axes, and hatchets; men die, bodies are defended or stripped of armor, and fighting centers around Alcathous. The struggle rages most fiercely by the wall and ships: the left wing favors the Argives, while the Trojans press the ships. Neptune’s cry strengthens the Achaeans, and after Hector is removed they gain confidence, though casualties fall on both sides. The course then reverses when Neptune withdraws and Apollo intervenes: Apollo’s aegis panics the Achaeans and the Trojans drive them back into a narrow space by the ships. Patroclus restores Achaean momentum and forces the Trojans back. Finally, the combat becomes scattered; chieftains kill one another, the Trojans lose formation and flee before a broad Danaan assault.

supports the Achaeans [by restoring their courage] Neptune’s intervention consists of secretly entering the Achaean side in human disguises, encouraging the warriors, and increasing their courage and strength. He first aids the two Ajaxes and other Achaeans, then urges Idomeneus and Meriones to rejoin the fighting.

l: the Achaean defensive formation, The Iliad
s: is_made_of spears and shields [densely serried] The Achaeans gather around the two Ajaxes in a tightly serried formation, with spear, shield, buckler, helmet, and man pressed closely together. This living fence prevents Hector from continuing easily through the tents and ships and drives him back for a time.

Spears dominate the close combat: Idomeneus kills Othryoneus, Asius, and Alcathous with one; Deiphobus kills Hypsenor and wounds Ascalaphus; and many others are wounded or killed by spears. Neptune makes Adamas’s spear ineffective against Antilochus, leaving part of it stuck in the shield.

l: ships of Ajax and Protesilaus, The Iliad
s: Ships drawn up by the sea-shore, defended by Achaeans where Hector first broke through the gates and wall; the low wall makes fighting around them especially fierce.

Sleep is a divine personification and brother of Death who fears Jupiter after punishment. Initially refusing Juno’s request, he accepts Pasithea as bride, hides on Mount Ida, puts Jupiter to sleep, and tells Neptune to aid the Danaans.

The Achaeans are in a disastrous retreat, flying pell-mell before the Trojans. Agamemnon proposes withdrawing the ships as part of the retreat, but Ulysses rejects the idea and Diomed urges the leaders to support the fighting men.

l: Hera’s deception of Jupiter, The Iliad
s: Juno deceives Jupiter by claiming that she is going to visit Oceanus and Tethys, obtaining Venus’s girdle, and arranging for Sleep to assist her. She then seduces Jupiter on Mount Ida, where Sleep causes him to fall into slumber.

contains love [among Venus’s charms] Venus’s girdle contains love, desire, and sweet flattery that can steal the judgment of even the most prudent. Venus gives it to Juno, who places it in her bosom and uses its charms in her plan to beguile Jupiter.

Agamemnon counsels drawing the ships into the water and escaping by night, but Ulysses condemns the proposal as destructive. Diomed instead counsels the wounded leaders to go near the battle and encourage the Achaeans while avoiding the spears.

l: Neptune's rallying of the Danaans, The Iliad
s: calls_for exchange of armour [to strengthen the army] Neptune urged the Danaans to support one another and resist Hector without waiting for Achilles. He told them to take the largest shields, put on their helmets, carry their longest spears, and exchange inferior armour for better equipment.

l: Hector's wounding and removal from battle, The Iliad
s: includes Hector son of Priam After Hector's spear failed against Ajax son of Telamon, Ajax struck him in the neck with a stone and knocked him down. Hector's comrades covered him with shields, carried him to his chariot, and took him to the ford of Xanthus, where he vomited blood, briefly recovered, and then lost consciousness again.
Armour includes shield, helmet, and long spear; Danaans exchange it so the most valiant receive the best, then don bronze armour and march to battle.

Neptune instructed the Danaans to take the best and largest shields available and to give smaller shields to worse men. Hector's shield and armour were fastened to him when he fell, and Trojan princes held their round shields over him to protect him.

Hector's spear struck Ajax son of Telamon but was stopped by the bands of Ajax's shield and sword. Spears killed or wounded several fighters, including Prothoenor, Promachus, Ilioneus, Satnius, and Hyperenor.

is_led_by Apollo [carrying the aegis before Hector and the Trojans] The Trojan advance begins after Apollo restores Hector and goes before the Trojan horses. It carries the Trojans across the trench and through the ruined wall as Hector leads them toward the Achaean ships.

is_caused_by Apollo [through Jove’s will] Hector’s recovery follows Apollo’s arrival after Hector has been struck by Ajax and left gasping, confused, and vomiting blood. Apollo restores his strength and breathing, enabling him to recognize those around him and return to battle.

is_caused_by Jove [after Iris delivers Jove’s threat] Neptune’s withdrawal occurs after Iris warns him that Jove is older and stronger and may attack him. He leaves the field and goes beneath the sea, and the Achaeans sorely miss his support.

supports the Trojan advance [by restoring Hector and panicking the Achaeans] Apollo’s intervention restores Hector, strengthens the Trojans, and terrifies the Achaeans. He carries the aegis, leads the Trojan advance, opens the trench, and destroys the Achaean wall.

An Achaean ship that brought Protesilaus to Troy but did not return him becomes the focus of fierce fighting. Hector seizes its stern and orders fire; Trojans attack and ignite it. Patroclus kills Pyraechmes, drives them away, and quenches the flames, though the ship remains half-burnt.

The armour of Achilles is immortal armour given by the gods to Peleus and later to Achilles. Achilles lends it to Patroclus, who wears all but Achilles’ great spear so Trojans may mistake him for Achilles. After Patroclus falls, Hector takes, wears, and boasts in the armour, appearing like Achilles and leaving Achilles unable to arm himself. Later, Achilles again wears the gleaming armour while pursuing Hector; it protects him when Hector’s spear strikes the shield and rebounds without piercing it.

l: fire attack on the Achaean ships, The Iliad
s: Fire, set and used by the Trojans to attack the Achaean ships, becomes their immediate objective. Hector repeatedly orders it brought, but Ajax resists. After Hector cuts Ajax’s spear, the Trojans ignite a ship’s stern; Patroclus and the Myrmidons drive them back and quench it.

l: Patroclus’s mission to Achilles, The Iliad
s: is_a mission [to induce Achilles to fight] Patroclus’s mission is to leave Eurypylus and persuade Achilles to enter the fighting. He believes that a friend’s advice should be heeded and hopes that heaven may help him convince Achilles.

l: defense of the Achaean ships, The Iliad
s: depends_on hard fighting [because no outside help is available] Ajax, Nestor, Teucer, Menelaus, Antilochus, and other Achaeans organize a determined defense of the ships. They rely on close combat, mutual exhortation, and the conviction that their salvation depends on their own fighting.

l: honor and shame in battle, The Iliad
s: motivates Achaeans [to stand firm rather than flee] Hector tells the Trojans that dying while fighting for their country is honorable and will protect their families and property if the Achaeans are defeated. Ajax and Nestor likewise invoke shame, mutual respect, and the disgrace of flight to keep the Achaeans in the battle.

influences battle at the ships [by aiding the Trojans and hindering the Achaeans] Jove aids the Trojans by breaking Teucer’s bowstring, encouraging Hector, and weakening the Achaeans’ courage. Minerva lifts darkness from the Achaeans’ eyes, while Apollo prevents Polydamas from being struck by Meges.

Euphorbus is a Dardanian Trojan warrior, son of Panthous and famed as a spearman, horseman, and runner. He wounds Patroclus from behind, withdraws, then claims the first blow and challenges Menelaus. Menelaus kills him through the throat and strips his armour.

l: Patroclus's arming and deployment, The Iliad
s: includes Achilles’ armour [Patroclus puts it on] Patroclus puts on Achilles’ armour while Automedon yokes Xanthus, Balius, and Pedasus to his chariot. He is deployed at the head of the Myrmidons to rescue the Achaeans and the ships.

l: Patroclus's advance against the Trojans, The Iliad
s: Patroclus leads the Myrmidons against the Trojans near Protesilaus's ship, kills Pyraechmes, confuses the Paeonians, and helps drive the Trojans from the ships.

is_a vehicles [being smashed and abandoned during the rout] Chariots are smashed in all directions during the rout, and many men fall from their own cars beneath Patroclus's wheels. Some horses leave their masters' chariots behind after breaking the poles in the trench.

l: rout of the Trojans, The Iliad
s: has_state disordered [with panic and no remaining fight] The rout is panic-stricken and disordered, like a storm spreading over the earth. The Trojans fill the ways with cries, raise clouds of dust, and flee toward the city and the ships.

l: flight of the Trojans, The Iliad
s: is_a panic-stricken retreat [toward the city from the tents and ships] The Trojans' flight takes them away from the battle, but Patroclus heads his horses toward the places where they are most confused and prevents nearby battalions from reaching the city. Their retreat is accompanied by broken chariots, trapped horses, and falling men.
Death, paired with Sleep, closes dying Sarpedon’s eyes and carries his body to Lycia for burial.

Sarpedon asks Glaucus to prevent the Achaeans from taking his armour after his death. The Achaeans strip the gleaming armour from his shoulders, and Patroclus gives it to his men to carry to the ships.

is_stripped_of Sarpedon’s armour [by the Achaeans] Sarpedon’s body becomes the focus of a fierce battle between the Trojans and Lycians and the Myrmidons and Achaeans. After the Achaeans take his armour, Apollo removes the body from the fighting, cleanses it, clothes it in immortal raiment, and sends it with Death and Sleep to Lycia.

l: the battle over Sarpedon’s body, The Iliad
s: is_fought_by Trojans [against Lycians, Myrmidons, and Achaeans] The battle begins after Sarpedon’s death as both sides try to seize or defend his body and armour. The fighting is intensified by Jove’s darkness and results in many deaths before the Trojans and Lycians retreat and the Achaeans take the armour.

is_a death of a mortal favored by a god [under divine fate] Sarpedon’s death is caused by Patroclus’s spear thrust near his heart after Sarpedon misses twice. Jove pities him but accepts that his mortal death cannot be prevented, and he honours Sarpedon with a rain of blood.

takes_place_in Lycia [with mound and pillar in due honour] Sarpedon’s brothers and kinsmen are to bury him in Lycia with a mound and pillar, in due honour to the dead. Death and Sleep carry him there after Apollo prepares his body.

l: divine fate and mortal death, The Iliad
s: governs Sarpedon [his doom is fated] Juno states that a mortal man whose doom has long been fated should not be rescued from death, and Jove accepts this judgment concerning Sarpedon. The gods can influence the battle and prepare the dead, but Sarpedon still dies by Patroclus’s hand.

l: battle over Cebriones's body, The Iliad
s: The battle over Cebriones’s body pits Patroclus and Hector, with Achaeans and Trojans fighting fiercely; after weapons clash around the corpse, the Achaeans prevail, remove it, and strip its armour.

Fate and death govern mortals, decree Aeneas’s escape and the survival of the Dardanian line, and frame Achilles’s choice to remain at Troy for fame despite his imminent doom after Hector. Aeneas must avoid Achilles until Achilles dies, then may fight safely.

The body of Patroclus, after his death, becomes the center of a day-long struggle. Menelaus and Ajax guard it as Trojans seek to carry it to Ilius and Achaeans pull it toward their ships. Hector attacks and tries three times to drag it away, but the two Ajaxes repel him. After Achilles frightens the Trojans, the Achaeans recover, wash, anoint, and place the mangled body on a bier. In Achilles’s tent, comrades mourn while Thetis preserves it from decay.
Hector strips the armour from Patroclus after reaching his body. The text thereafter focuses on Hector’s possession of Achilles’ armour rather than on the armour taken from Patroclus.

is_a battle [between Trojans and Achaeans over Patroclus’s body] The body-removal struggle pits Hector and the Trojans against Ajax, Menelaus, and the Achaeans. The two sides repeatedly pull the body across a small area, with neither side yielding for the entire day.
Euphorbus dies when Menelaus drives a spear through his throat. Menelaus then strips his armour, but Apollo’s intervention brings Hector against him before he can carry it away.

l: battle for Patroclus's body, The Iliad
s: The battle for Patroclus’s body is a fight near the ships between Achaeans and Trojans: the Trojans seek to carry the body to Ilius, while the Achaeans seek to take it to their ships. Fighting continues from Menelaus and Euphorbus through massed combat with spears, swords, and chariots. Ajax organizes the defense; Hector repeatedly tries to seize the body. Jove and Minerva influence the struggle, until Achilles’s appearance confuses the Trojans.

l: rescue of Patroclus's body, The Iliad
s: is_attempted_by Achaeans [Menelaus and Meriones carry the body while the two Ajaxes cover them] Menelaus and Meriones lift Patroclus's body and carry it toward the ships while the two Ajaxes protect them. The Trojans pursue fiercely, but the two Ajaxes repeatedly face them and hold back the attack as the rescuers strain to escape.

l: the city of Priam, The Iliad
s: is_also_called Ilius

l: Achilles’s return to battle, The Iliad
s: Achilles resolves to return to battle after Patroclus’s death, although he lacks armour and Thetis has told him to wait. At Iris’s urging, he shows himself at the trench; Minerva surrounds him with the aegis and a fiery glow, and his cry causes the Trojans to flee and allows the Achaeans to recover Patroclus’s body.

Mourning for Patroclus is a collective grief centered on Achilles after Patroclus’s death. Achilles expresses it with dust, tears, torn hair, lamentation, refusal of food, and thoughts of slaughter and blood. The Myrmidons, Achaeans, captive bondswomen, and Briseis join the mourning, with Briseis and the women also lamenting their own losses. Achilles leads all-night lamentation, circles Patroclus’s body in chariots, cuts his hair, pours wine onto the ground, and calls on Patroclus until the pyre burns down. Later, grief over other dead drives Priam to seek Hector’s body.

l: the armour made by Vulcan, The Iliad
s: Vulcan’s armour is a divine-made set for Achilles: a great, strong, richly worked shield; a breastplate brighter than fire; a close-fitting helmet with golden plume; greaves of beaten tin; and, when given, a sword. After Achilles loses his former armour when Patroclus falls, Thetis asks Vulcan to forge new armour. She promises its arrival, carries it to Achilles at daybreak, and gives it to him. The Myrmidons recoil in awe; Achilles puts it on, and it seems to buoy him up like wings.
Vulcan's house is an imperishable, star-bespangled bronze place in heaven, made by Vulcan, containing his forge, tools, wheeled tripods, and immortal-like golden handmaids.

Newly made for Achilles, the shield is made by Vulcan five layers thick, with a gleaming threefold rim and silver baldric. It depicts earth, heaven, sea, constellations, two cities and their battle, fields, harvest, vineyard, cattle, pasture, dancers, musicians, and Oceanus around its outer rim. It ends as a huge, strong, brilliant shield whose firelike light shines into heaven when Achilles carries it into battle.

The armor requested for Achilles consists of a helmet, shield, greaves fitted with ankle-clasps, and a breastplate. Vulcan makes the pieces from copper, tin, silver, and gold, and the finished work is made to amaze all who behold it.

l: reconciliation between Achilles and Agamemnon, The Iliad
s: is_between Achilles and Agamemnon Achilles and Agamemnon are reconciled.
is_battle_of Achilles Achilles goes out to fight.
Achilles throws his spear at Hector, but Hector avoids it; Minerva retrieves it and returns it to Achilles. Achilles then uses it to strike Hector in the throat and later draws it from the body.

l: the ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad
s: are_near Ilius [outside the city] The Achaean ships are the destination of Priam's journey and the place where Achilles and the Myrmidons are encamped. Priam reaches them under Mercury's protection without being seen by the Achaeans.

is_attended_by Achaean heroes [after Achilles summons them] The assembly gathers after Achilles calls the Achaean heroes. Achilles and Agamemnon speak there about their quarrel, Agamemnon's gifts and oath are presented, and Achilles finally breaks it up so the men can prepare to fight.
Agamemnon's oath calls Jove, Earth, Sun, and the Erinyes to witness that he never touched Briseis sexually or otherwise. He makes the oath before the Achaeans and sacrifices a boar.

l: the funeral of Patroclus, The Iliad
s: Patroclus’s funeral proceeds through communal mourning, a feast, hair-cutting, construction and burning of a pyre with extensive sacrifices and offerings, then placement of his bones in a golden urn, raising of a burial mound, and funeral games with prizes.

l: the fate of Achilles, The Iliad
s: determines Achilles' death [together with a man and a god] Divine fate is presented as governing human suffering and death: Thetis says Patroclus fell by heaven's will, Agamemnon blames Jove, Fate, and Erinys for his madness, and Xanthus tells Achilles that heaven and stern fate will bring about his death.

is_a hill [overlooking the battle] Callicolone is the hill where the gods supporting the Trojans sit and watch the battle. Mars calls to the Trojans from its side, and the gods use its brow as a vantage point.
The barrow of Hercules is a high masonry earth-barrow made by Trojans and Pallas Minerva, serving Hercules as refuge and sheltering gods watching battle.

l: council of the gods, The Iliad
s: is_a council The council of the gods is convened by Jove through Themis. At the council, Jove explains that he will watch from Olympus while the other gods take sides in the battle.

l: battle between gods and mortals, The Iliad
s: The gods influence the battle between the Achaeans and Trojans by encouraging, warning, and protecting individual warriors. Their own rivalries produce thunder, earthquakes, and loud cries, but they largely refrain from directly fighting one another.

l: fight between Achilles and Aeneas, The Iliad
s: Achilles and Aeneas exchange boasts about their ancestry before throwing their spears. Aeneas’s spear cannot penetrate Achilles’ divinely made shield, while Achilles’ spear pierces Aeneas’s shield. Achilles is about to kill Aeneas, but Neptune interrupts the fight and carries Aeneas away.

l: Neptune's rescue of Aeneas, The Iliad
s: is_a rescue [divine intervention] Neptune saves Aeneas when Achilles is about to kill him. He places darkness before Achilles’ eyes, removes Achilles’ spear from Aeneas’s shield, carries Aeneas beyond the battle, and tells him that his survival is required by fate.

l: Achilles' slaughter of the Trojans, The Iliad
s: is_a slaughter [carried out in battle] After Aeneas is removed from the fight, Achilles urges the Achaeans to attack. He advances against the Trojans and kills Iphition by splitting his head in two, while the text states that he kills many Trojans.

protects Aeneas [from Achilles in battle] Aeneas recognizes that Achilles is repeatedly protected by a god, while Apollo encourages Aeneas and Neptune ultimately saves him. Achilles is also supported by the gods allied with the Achaeans, who consider strengthening him against the Trojans.

Polydorus, Priam’s youngest and most loved son and fastest runner, is forbidden to fight. He disobeys, runs among the front ranks, and Achilles strikes him through the back to the navel; he dies holding his entrails.

l: the fight between Achilles and the river, The Iliad
s: is_a conflict The fight begins when Xanthus, angered by the corpses in its waters, attacks Achilles with rising floods and pursues him across the plain. Achilles struggles to escape, aided by Neptune and Minerva, while Xanthus calls on Simois for help. Juno sends Vulcan, whose fire overwhelms and forces Xanthus to yield.

l: the battle among the gods, The Iliad
s: A conflict and quarrel among gods of divided counsels during the struggle around Xanthus. It begins when Mars attacks Minerva; Minerva defeats Mars and Venus, Juno defeats Diana, while Neptune and Apollo refrain. Xanthus attacks Achilles but submits after Vulcan’s fire prevails.

protects the Trojans [by Apollo’s aid] Divine intervention repeatedly changes the fighting. Juno stops the fight involving Xanthus, Minerva and Juno defeat other gods, and Apollo protects the Trojans by saving Agenor and deceiving Achilles.

Hector's death is a battle episode caused by Achilles. Achilles pursues Hector three times around the city; Zeus weighs their dooms, Hector's falls toward Hades, and Minerva tricks him into stopping. Achilles kills Hector with a spear through the throat, treats the victory as a triumph, and considers the next attack. Hector's loss leaves Troy and Ilius without their principal, bravest defender, prompting citywide lament and Priam's attempt to recover his body.

Hector’s body is a dead body whose treatment after Hector’s death centers on Achilles’ dishonour and the gods’ protection. Achilles strips it of armor; Achaeans gather around and spear it. Its feet are pierced and tied to Achilles’ chariot, which drags it toward the ships with its head in the dust. Achilles lays it beside Patroclus’s bier, threatens it with dogs, drags it around Patroclus’s tomb, and leaves it near his tent. Venus prevents dogs from tearing it, while Apollo protects it from heat and disfigurement; after twelve days, the immortals keep it fresh, unwasted, and free from worms. Priam ransoms it, and Achilles releases it. The body is washed, anointed, clothed, carried on a bier by mules to Troy, displayed for mourning, burned, placed in a golden urn, and buried beneath a barrow.

Hector’s funeral rites are the promised return and burial of Hector’s corpse, despite Achilles’ earlier refusal to allow proper rites. The Achaeans give back the body, enabling Priam’s plan: nine days of mourning and gathering wood, burning and burying Hector on the tenth day, and raising a burial mound on the eleventh. His bones are placed in a golden urn, the grave is covered with stones, and a funeral feast is held in Priam’s house.

l: Hector's family and mourners, The Iliad
s: Hector’s parents, wife, relatives, and the people of the city grieve openly over his death. His wife’s sisters and her brothers’ wives support her after she faints, while the people join the family’s lament.

l: Hector's dragging and dishonour, The Iliad
s: Achilles dishonours Hector by tying his corpse to the chariot and dragging it through the dust toward the Achaean ships. Hector’s family and the Trojans witness or hear of this treatment and respond with intense grief.

l: the Trojan lament for Hector, The Iliad
s: The Trojan lament is the city’s collective mourning for Hector. It begins when his parents see his body dragged away, with Hecuba and his wife grieving his death, dishonour, and Astyanax’s future. When his body reaches Troy, Andromache, Hecuba, Helen, and the crowd mourn his family, kindness, protection, and importance.
Patroclus's spirit, a ghost, appears in Achilles' dream seeking swift burial and shared bones, warning that Achilles too will die beneath Troy's walls.

After Patroclus's cremation and burial preparations, Achilles convenes an assembly and brings out prizes for the funeral games. The prizes include cauldrons, tripods, horses, mules, oxen, women with fair girdles, and iron. The funeral contests for Patroclus include the chariot races and prizes for the competitors. Achilles continues the observance by distributing prizes and honoring Nestor with an urn as a memorial of Patroclus.
A hundred-foot-square wooden pyre holds Patroclus, animals, captives, honey, and unguents; after Achilles prays to Boreas and Zephyrus, winds kindle and sustain its flames through the night.

covers golden urn [after the urn was placed in the tent] The Achaeans mark out a circle, lay a foundation, and heap earth into a burial mound for Patroclus. Achilles initially asks that it be of reasonable size, with a larger mound to be completed later by the Achaeans after his death.

Chariot races are held as funeral contests for Patroclus, with five prizes for finishers. Diomed wins; Antilochus finishes ahead of Menelaus through a disputed maneuver; Meriones is fourth; and Eumelus, thrown from his chariot, finishes last.
The boxing contest offers a strong she-mule to the victor and a double cup to the vanquished. Epeus strikes Euryalus on the jaw, wins the mule, and Euryalus is carried away swooning.

The wrestling contest offers a twelve-oxen tripod to the winner and a skilled enslaved woman to the loser. Ajax son of Telamon and Ulysses cannot defeat each other; Achilles stops their renewed struggle and awards equal prizes.

is_given_to Nestor [as an heirloom and memorial of Patroclus] The two-handled urn is the fifth prize in the chariot races and is described as unsoiled by smoke. Since it remains unawarded, Achilles gives it to Nestor as an heirloom and memorial of Patroclus's funeral.

The chariots race across the plain toward a turning-post, with drivers standing and urging their horses onward. Eumelus's chariot is damaged when his yoke breaks, while Diomed's gold-and-tin-inlaid chariot reaches the finish with little trace of wheel-marks in the dust.

l: Epeus son of Panopeus, The Iliad
s: Epeus, son of Panopeus, is a brave, large, skilful champion boxer. He claims superiority, challenges the competitors, defeats Euryalus with a jaw blow, helps him up, and wins the she-mule.

has_prize mixing-bowl [for the swiftest runner] The speed-running contest offers a silver mixing-bowl for first place, a fat ox for second, and half a talent of gold for last place. Ajax son of Oileus leads initially, but Ulysses wins with Minerva's help after Ajax slips on cattle offal, while Antilochus takes the last prize.

A beautifully worked silver vessel from Sidon, made by cunning artificers and brought by Phoenicians from beyond the sea, holds six measures; Achilles offers it as a running-contest prize, and Ulysses wins it.

seeks_to_recover Hector's corpse [by offering gifts to Achilles] Priam’s ransom mission is set in motion by Jove’s command that he go to the Achaean ships and recover Hector’s body. Priam plans to travel with only an honored servant, carrying valuable gifts for Achilles.

The ransom gifts are Priam’s treasure offered to Achilles for Hector’s body: garments, gold, tripods, cauldrons, and a precious cup. Priam gathers and loads them onto a waggon, and Mercury brings them into Achilles’ dwelling. Achilles accepts the ransom, judges it not unworthy, and says it will be shared equitably with Patroclus; Hector’s body is released and wrapped in mantles and a shirt.

l: divine justice and restraint, The Iliad
s: opposes Achilles [because he dishonours the dead] The gods condemn Achilles’ continued mistreatment of Hector’s dead body and urge restraint toward the dead. Jove balances honor for Achilles with respect for Hector by ordering that Hector’s body be released through ransom.

is_built_for Achilles [by the Myrmidons] Achilles' tent is a lofty dwelling built by the Myrmidons and enclosed by a fenced courtyard with a heavy barred gate. Mercury brings Priam and the treasure inside, where Priam finds Achilles seated with his men.

is_escorted_by Mercury [by order of Jove] The journey to Achilles begins when Priam leaves Ilius with Idaeus, mules, horses, and a ransom. Mercury guides and protects them across the plain and through the Achaean defenses until Priam reaches Achilles' tent.

l: the ransom of Hector, The Iliad
s: is_offered_by Priam's treasure [to Achilles] The ransom of Hector consists of rich treasure carried by Priam to Achilles' tent. Priam offers it in exchange for Hector's body, but Achilles says he is already minded to return the body.
Mourning fills Achilles' house as Priam grieves Hector and Achilles grieves Peleus and Patroclus; Achilles says grief cannot restore the dead, though Priam must mourn.

This document is The Odyssey, tracing Ulysses’ return from Troy, his son Telemachus’s search for him, and the recovery of Ulysses’ household in Ithaca. Ulysses is detained by Calypso while the gods, led by Jove and aided by Minerva, decide he must go home; Neptune remains hostile because Ulysses blinded his son Polyphemus. Minerva first strengthens Telemachus, who confronts Penelope’s suitors and travels to Pylos and Lacedaemon. Nestor, Menelaus, and Helen confirm Ulysses’ importance and suffering, while the suitors, led especially by Antinous, plot to kill Telemachus. Mercury orders Calypso to release Ulysses. After Neptune wrecks his raft, Ulysses reaches Scheria, where Nausicaa, Alcinous, Arete, and the Phaeacians receive him. At Alcinous’s court, Ulysses reveals himself and recounts his long wanderings: disasters among the Cicons and Lotus-eaters; escape from Polyphemus, whose prayer brings Neptune’s vengeance; Aeolus’s winds; the Laestrygonians; Circe; the journey to Hades and Teiresias’s warnings; the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis; and the destruction of his crew after they kill Hyperion’s cattle. Alone, he reaches Calypso. The Phaeacians finally carry Ulysses to Ithaca. Minerva disguises him as a beggar, and he finds loyalty in Eumaeus the swineherd. Telemachus returns safely, meets his disguised father, and joins him in planning against the suitors. In the palace, Ulysses endures insults, is recognized by his dog Argos and later by Euryclea through an old scar, but keeps his identity hidden. Penelope, still faithful despite the suitors’ pressure, announces that whoever can string Ulysses’ bow and shoot through twelve axes will marry her. Ulysses strings the bow effortlessly, reveals himself, and with Telemachus, Eumaeus, Philoetius, and Minerva kills the suitors. The disloyal women and Melanthius are punished, and the house is purified. Penelope accepts Ulysses only after he proves knowledge of their immovable bed. In the end, Ulysses reunites with Laertes; when Eupeithes leads Ithacans against him, Laertes kills Eupeithes, and Minerva and Jove impose peace.
Muse is a divine daughter of Olympian Jove who inspires, teaches, and loves bards, grants song, and is invoked to tell Ulysses’ travels and sufferings.

Ulysses is a mortal man, king of Ithaca, son of Laertes, husband of Penelope, and father of Telemachus: an Achaean hero renowned for subtlety, counsel, courage, endurance, archery, and concern for his homeland. He fights at Troy, enters it in disguise, and is among those in the wooden horse. After Troy falls, he leads his men toward Ithaca, but their folly, hostile seas, monsters, shipwrecks, and prolonged wandering destroy them all. He survives alone, though detained unwillingly by Calypso and continually longing for Penelope, Telemachus, and Ithaca. Freed to leave Calypso, he builds a raft, survives a storm, and reaches the Phaeacians, where Nausicaa, Alcinous, and others receive him as a distressed stranger. There he tells of his travels: deceiving and escaping Polyphemus as “Noman,” losing ships and companions, overcoming Circe’s threat, consulting Teiresias among the dead, hearing the Sirens while bound to the mast, and surviving Scylla, Charybdis, and a final shipwreck. The Phaeacians send him home with gifts. Returned to Ithaca after twenty years, he hides his treasure and, with Minerva’s aid, becomes an aged, ragged beggar. He tests loyalties, reveals himself to Telemachus, and plans against the suitors occupying his house and courting Penelope. He endures insults and concealment until the contest of his bow. He strings it, shoots through the iron, kills the suitors with Telemachus, and orders the house cleansed. His story moves from celebrated warrior and lost king, through suffering wanderer and suppliant, to disguised homecomer reclaiming his household.

Troy is Priam’s city, containing a Trojan fortress, and the enemy city besieged by the Achaeans for nine years. During the war, the disguised Ulysses gathers information there and serves in an ambush near its walls; Neoptolemus fights bravely, kills Eurypylus and many others, and enters the horse made by Epeus. After the Trojans debate the wooden horse and receive it inside the fortress, the city is doomed. In the tenth year, repeated stratagems lead the Achaeans to sack and ravage Troy, with Ulysses among its sackers. Neoptolemus receives spoils, while losses there remain a source of grief and may include brave relations or comrades. After the fall, Ulysses and his men, and the divided Achaeans, begin troubled return voyages from Troy.

Ulysses’s men are the companions and crew of his ship, commanded by Ulysses. Their course is marked by shared labor, repeated losses, and fatal folly. They raid Ismarus and divide booty fairly, but refuse to leave when ordered, suffer losses against the Cicons, and some eat lotus and lose the desire to return. They escape the Cyclops after warning Ulysses against further provocation, mourn lost comrades, and continue sailing. Suspicious that an ox-hide sack holds treasure, they open it while Ulysses sleeps. After six windless days, Laestrygonians kill all men in the harbor except those aboard Ulysses’s ship. On Circe’s island, some are changed into pigs but retain human senses; Circe restores them, and the company remains eating and drinking for a year. They later urge return home, follow orders toward Hades, bury Elpenor, seal their ears with wax, bind Ulysses to the mast, and row past the Sirens. Finally, despite the danger and their oath, they slaughter the Sun-god’s cattle. Jove destroys their ship, and the surviving crew are killed in the shipwreck.

l: the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion, The Odyssey
s: Hyperion’s beloved cattle are a fair, protected, unchanging herd on Thrinacian island: seven herds of fifty, tended by Phaethusa and Lampetie. Though warned to spare them, Ulysses’s crew kills the best when food fails, after which hides crawl and meat lows.
owns the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion Hyperion is identified as the sun-god and as the father of Phaethusa and Lampetie by Neaera.

Calypso is an immortal, great and powerful goddess and nymph, daughter of Atlas, who dwells in a cave on the Ogygian island. After Ulysses is stranded there, she receives and cares for him, but becomes his unwilling lover, wants to marry him, and keeps him prisoner for seven years, trying to make him forget home. Though she can make him immortal and ageless, his lack of ships and sailors also prevents his return. Mercury brings her Jove’s judgment that Ulysses must leave. Calypso releases him, helps him build a raft, supplies clothing and provisions, sends a favorable wind, and warns that he will suffer greatly on the journey.

Ithaca is a rugged, productive island and country: Ulysses’s homeland, the home of Telemachus, Penelope, and their household, and the setting of Ulysses’ estate, house, city, harbour, Neritum, Eumaeus’s hut and pig yards, and Laertes’s farm. Though it lacks open fields and racecourses and is better for goats than horses, it has corn, wine, cattle, goats, timber, rain, dew, and unfailing watering places. Its greatest importance is as the home to which Ulysses longs to return and as the property endangered during his absence. While he is away, suitors consume his estate and household while courting Penelope; Telemachus leaves from Ithaca seeking news, then returns despite their attempted interception. Ulysses repeatedly names Ithaca as his dearest country and intended destination, though prophecy makes his return dependent on suffering and the loss of his men. He finally reaches the island by ship, initially fails to recognize it in mist, and moves through it in disguise, staying with Eumaeus before approaching his household. After twenty years, he returns openly enough to recover his home and kill the suitors. Their deaths divide Ithaca’s people, but Minerva brings peace.

The immortal gods are blessed divine beings, everlasting and living in everlasting bliss, who govern much of mortal fortune, travel, safety, punishment, and fate. They require hecatombs and sacrifices as their dues, detaining Menelaus in Egypt until these obligations are met and determining his life after death in the Elysian plain. At the beginning, they meet in Jove’s house to discuss Ulysses, whom all except Neptune pity, and decide that he should return; Minerva and Mercury are assigned to aid his departure and household. They determine whether Ulysses will return and take revenge, though they cannot cross Jove or disobey his orders. Their actions both assist and afflict him: they send favorable wind, signs, dangers, a shipwreck punishing the slaughter of the sun-god’s cattle, and his stranding on Ogygian island, while later decreeing his release from Calypso. They arrange the Argive Danaans’ misfortunes for future song, control Telemachus’s safety, and are invoked by Eumaeus and consulted by the suitors as Minerva aids Ulysses and his household.

Neptune is a sea god, king of the sea, Lord of the Earthquake, and holder of a trident used to stir the sea. He has a palace at Aegae and is father of Polyphemus, the Cyclops, Nausithous, and the Cyclops more broadly. His central action is relentless anger toward Ulysses, chiefly because Ulysses blinded Polyphemus. While away among the Ethiopians, Neptune prevents Ulysses from returning home despite the other gods’ intention to help. Seeing Ulysses near Phaeacia, he raises a violent storm and destroys his raft; Ulysses also fears further sea-born danger from him. Neptune hears the Cyclops’s prayer, and the Cyclops’s second thrown rock drives Ulysses’s ship shoreward. Teiresias warns that Neptune will continue to make Ulysses’s return difficult, until Ulysses later sacrifices to him. Neptune is also angry with the Phaeacians for readily escorting travelers. After they bring Ulysses home with gifts, he turns their returning ship to stone and drives it into the ground near Scheria, after having threatened their city with burial beneath a high mountain.

Jove is a god, son of Saturn, king and chief of the gods and men, ruler of heaven and earth, and lord of all. He is married to Juno and is father of Minerva and, as stated by Vulcan, Venus. As guardian of suppliants, strangers, beggars, foreigners in distress, and hospitality, he is invoked in prayers and as a witness. He governs events by divine will, sometimes bringing misfortune, panic, storms, shipwreck, and destruction by thunderbolt. At the gods’ meeting, he explains Neptune’s persecution of Ulysses and supports planning Ulysses’ return. Later he decrees that Ulysses return home without divine or human convoy, orders Mercury to command Calypso to release him, and declares that the Phaeacians will honor and transport him. He agrees to punish Ulysses’ crew for slaughtering the sun-god’s cattle, then raises a storm and destroys their ship, killing the men. He answers Ulysses’ request for a sign with thunder and hears the miller-woman’s prayer against the suitors. At the end, he supports peace: Ulysses is to continue ruling, opponents are to forgive the massacre, and a fiery thunderbolt reinforces Minerva’s command to end the war.

Aegisthus is a murderer and ruler of Mycenae whose central acts are seducing Clytemnestra and killing her husband Agamemnon. Despite Mercury’s warning, he removes the bard guarding Agamemnon’s wife, wins Clytemnestra by persistent flattery, and learns of Agamemnon’s return. He welcomes Agamemnon with a feast or banquet, ambushes and kills him and his companions, then rules in Mycene for seven years. Orestes, Agamemnon’s son, eventually returns and kills Aegisthus in revenge, bringing the consequences of Aegisthus’s actions upon him.

Agamemnon, son of Atreus and brother of Menelaus, is king of the Argives and a leader among the Achaeans after Troy. He urges waiting to sacrifice to Minerva before the homeward voyage, survives the voyage, and reaches Argos. There Aegisthus, allied with Agamemnon’s wife Clytemnestra, deceives him with a banquet and murders him in his house. Among the dead in Hades, Agamemnon recounts the treachery, asks after Orestes, mourns distrust born of his wife’s betrayal, and praises Penelope’s faithfulness. Menelaus preserves his memory with a barrow; Agamemnon also hears of his own mourning, funeral, and tomb.
Orestes, son of Agamemnon, returns from Athens eight years after his father’s death, kills Aegisthus in revenge, and holds funeral rites for his mother and Aegisthus.

Mercury is a god, messenger of the gods, guide and guardian, often appearing as a beautiful young man. With his golden wand, which can induce sleep or wake people, he warns Aegisthus in good will and carries Jove’s command to Calypso, demanding Ulysses’s release. He protects Ulysses from Circe by giving him Moly and instructions, assists Hercules in bringing the hell-hound from Hades, and endows Autolycus with a gift. At the end, as guide of the dead, he summons the suitors’ ghosts and leads them to the abode of death and before Agamemnon and Achilles.

Minerva is an immortal goddess, Jove’s daughter, who dwells on Olympus and is a protective, changeable divine ally of Ulysses and his family. She favors Ulysses from the Trojan War onward, assists in major earlier deeds, and repeatedly uses disguises, a golden wand, mist, winds, sleep, beauty, courage, and battle aid to advance his return and restore his household. At the beginning, concerned by Ulysses’ suffering on Calypso’s island and Neptune’s persecution, she presses for help and goes to Ithaca as Mentes and Mentor to strengthen Telemachus. She directs him to call an assembly, confront the suitors, and seek news of his father; she arranges and protects his voyage, later recalls him from Lacedaemon, and warns him of the suitors’ ambush. Meanwhile she aids Ulysses at sea, protects Nausicaa, guides him among the Phaeacians, and helps secure his passage home. Back in Ithaca, she conceals and disguises Ulysses, coordinates plans with him and Telemachus, directs him to Eumaeus, and prepares the downfall of the suitors. She also comforts and enhances Penelope, influences the bow contest, and gives Ulysses strength and protection during the fight, while making the suitors’ weapons ineffective. After the suitors are destroyed, she restores Laertes’ strength, directs his attack, and finally intervenes in the civil conflict to halt bloodshed and establish peace between the contending parties.

The Ogygian island is a lonely, sea-girt, forest-covered island in the middle of the sea, far from Ulysses’s friends. It contains Calypso’s beautiful cave, vineyards, birds, streams, and flowering plants. Calypso takes in and keeps Ulysses there in sorrow; he eventually leaves after building a raft, only to be stranded there again by the gods.

Polyphemus is a huge, inhuman Cyclops, king of the Cyclopes, son of Neptune and Thoosa, and a lawless outlaw who lives alone in a cave, shepherding sheep and goats. Resembling a mountain crag and carrying a massive olive-wood club, he rejects gods, laws, social order, and hospitality, eating six of Ulysses’s men rather than welcoming them. Ulysses makes him drunk and blinds his single eye; because Ulysses calls himself “Noman,” Polyphemus cannot identify the escaping men. Furious, he hurls rocks at Ulysses’s ship, recognizes an old prophecy has been fulfilled, and prays to Neptune for vengeance and healing. His blinding keeps Neptune angry with Ulysses.

Cyclopes are inhuman people who live in mountain-top caves. They neither plant nor plough, instead living on wild wheat, barley, and grapes. They have no laws, assemblies, ships, shipwrights, or travel between cities or overseas; each governs his own family. They receive prophecies from Telemus until he grows old. When Polyphemus cries out, neighboring Cyclopes come but leave after misunderstanding him.

Telemachus is the son of Ulysses and Penelope, Ulysses’s only son, heir, and eventual master of his Ithacan household and lands. At the beginning, the suitors consume his estate and abuse his home while Ulysses is absent; Telemachus doubts and seeks confirmation of his father’s fate but is urged by Minerva to act. He summons an assembly, publicly demands that the suitors leave, and secretly prepares a ship, crew, and provisions to seek news in Pylos and Sparta. He travels first to Pylos, where he is Nestor’s guest and is directed toward Menelaus, then goes by chariot with Pisistratus to Lacedaemon. There Menelaus and Helen recognize him as Ulysses’s son. Telemachus describes the ruin of his household and insists on truthful news of Ulysses. Though he is received comfortably and given gifts, he departs with Pisistratus, takes Theoclymenus aboard at Pylos, and sails home. During his absence, the suitors plot to kill him before he returns, but he reaches Ithaca safely, avoids their danger, and visits Eumaeus. At the swineherd’s station, Telemachus learns that Ulysses is his father and joins him in planning revenge. He keeps Ulysses’s identity secret, returns to Penelope and the household, and increasingly asserts authority over the suitors. He protects the disguised Ulysses as far as he can, condemns insults and violence, and openly warns the suitors that he will no longer endure the household’s disgrace. With Ulysses he removes and conceals the armour, controls access to Ulysses’s bow, and, though unable to string it himself, yields the contest at Ulysses’s signal. In the final struggle, Telemachus arms himself, kills Amphinomus and other suitors, brings weapons for Ulysses, and helps clear the household afterward. He seeks mercy for Phemius and Medon, keeps faith with Ulysses’s plans, and continues beside him in the Ithacan civil conflict, declaring that he will not disgrace his family. His course is from an aggrieved but hesitant heir to a shrewd, bold ally who helps recover and defend his father’s house.

Penelope is Ulysses’s wife, Telemachus’s mother, Icarius’s daughter, and queen of Ithaca and Ulysses’s household. During Ulysses’s long absence, she remains in his house with her maids, mourns and weeps for him continually, and suffers as the suitors consume his property and press her to remarry. Her central concern is loyalty to Ulysses and protection of their household and son. She learns of the plot against Telemachus, grieves, prays to Minerva for him, and is comforted by a dream promising his return. She rebukes the suitors for their conduct, seeks revenge upon them, protects guests from their mistreatment, and questions travelers and a stranger for news of Ulysses. Though pressured by her father, brothers, and the suitors, she postpones remarriage by weaving Laertes’s burial pall by day and secretly unpicking it at night for three years. In distress and uncertainty, she dreams, prays for release from misery, and finally sets the contest of Ulysses’s bow and twelve axes as the condition for choosing a husband. After the slaughter of the suitors, she does not immediately accept Ulysses’s return. She tests him by speaking of their bed; when he proves knowledge shared only by them and one maidservant, she recognizes and embraces him, and they share the sufferings of his absence.

The suitors are a group of 108 chiefly men from Ithaca and neighboring islands, led especially by Antinous and Eurymachus, who occupy Ulysses’ house while seeking to marry Penelope against her will. For three years they consume Ulysses’s and Telemachus’s livestock, wine, food, and household wealth without payment, hold lavish banquets, abuse hospitality, mistreat servants and guests, and dishonor Penelope and Telemachus through pride and insolence. Though Telemachus summons them to leave, they refuse until Penelope chooses a husband. They mock and threaten him, then plot to kill him as he returns from Pylos and Lacedaemon, waiting at sea to ambush him. Their conduct increasingly draws warnings and omens: Halitherses predicts Ulysses’ return, Teiresias foretells their deaths, Penelope dreams of geese killed by an eagle, and other signs announce destruction. While Ulysses is disguised as a stranger, they insult and attack him, though some give him food. They continue courting Penelope, give her gifts, expose her weaving ruse, and fail collectively to string Ulysses’s bow. After Ulysses strings it and shoots through the axe handles, he kills Antinous. The suitors try to escape and fight with armour supplied by Melanthius, but Minerva turns aside most of their weapons, and Ulysses and his allies kill them all. Their bodies are removed or buried, the house is purified, and their deaths lead Eupeithes and others to seek revenge.

The Achaeans are Agamemnon’s people, also called Danaans, who fight the Trojans in the Trojan War. They endure severe losses at Troy, where some burn their tents and depart while others hide with Ulysses inside a wooden horse within the Trojan fortress. Emerging from it, they sack and ravage Troy. After the city falls, they divide over immediate departure or sacrifices, and their homeward voyage brings storms, quarrels, divine displeasure, and many deaths. Some remain alive but cannot return, while a group led by Odysseus loses six men to Polyphemus before blinding him and escaping.
Sparta is another destination in Telemachus's planned search for news of Ulysses. Telemachus says he will travel there if he can obtain a ship and crew.

Pylos is a city, ruled by Nestor, containing Nestor’s house, and described as a land of sheep. It is a chief destination in Telemachus’s search for Ulysses: Minerva directs him to go there, and Antinous notes his intended departure. In Pylos, the people gather by the shore to sacrifice black bulls to Neptune, and Nestor and his people welcome Telemachus and Minerva. Telemachus later leaves its high citadel with Pisistratus for Lacedaemon, returns there to part from Pisistratus, takes aboard Theoclymenus, and finally sails back from Pylos with his crew.

Ulysses’s return is his long-sought homecoming to Ithaca after the homeward voyage, a return desired by Ulysses, Eumaeus, and Philoetius and decreed by the gods. It depends on endurance and restraint: Teiresias and Circe warn that harming the Sun’s flocks will cost Ulysses his companions and make the journey difficult, while leaving them unharmed may allow Ithaca after hardship. Earlier progress is repeatedly delayed, including by released winds and losses at Telepylus. Calypso predicts suffering, but Ulysses remains determined to see Penelope, his property, bondsmen, and household again. The Phaeacians ultimately enable the return, preparing a ship and carrying him while he sleeps. He is set down with his gifts near the harbour of Phorcys; Minerva conceals his arrival and directs him to remain unknown. Though reports and predictions of his approach are doubted by Eumaeus and Penelope, Ulysses is already in Ithaca, enters his house disguised, and is recognized only by Argos. After twenty years, he reveals himself to Eumaeus, Philoetius, Telemachus, and finally Laertes, proving his identity. The return restores him to his household, culminates in the suitors’ slaughter, and is followed by an Ithacan civil conflict when the deaths become known.

l: the blinding of Polyphemus, The Odyssey
s: The blinding of Polyphemus is Ulysses’ attack on the king of the Cyclopes. After getting him drunk and asleep, Odysseus and four companions drive a heated, sharpened olive-wood beam into his eye. Polyphemus’s cry that “Noman” attacks him misleads other Cyclopes. The injury cannot be healed except by Neptune and provokes Neptune’s continuing anger, obstructing Ulysses’ journey home.

l: the killing of Agamemnon, The Odyssey
s: The killing of Agamemnon occurs after his return home from Troy. Aegisthus allies with Clytemnestra, removes Agamemnon’s bard, invites Agamemnon to a banquet, and kills him after the feast; both sides’ followers die, and Menelaus later raises a barrow.

The Trojan War is a conflict fought at Troy, or Ilius, between the Achaeans and the Trojans. It involves Achaeans led by Ulysses with Idomeneus; the people of Crete demand that they lead ships in the expedition. After nine years of fighting, the city is taken in the tenth year. The war brings harassment, deaths among many Achaeans, destruction and suffering at Troy, and exploits by Ulysses and other warriors. Ulysses serves loyally, makes sacrifices to Neptune before Troy, sacks Troy, and later suffers while travelling from the conflict.

l: the suitors’ abuse of Telemachus’s household, The Odyssey
s: The suitors’ abuse of Telemachus’s household is a continuing pattern of wastefulness, mistreatment, and dishonor during Ulysses’s absence. They repeatedly occupy the house, sacrifice and consume its livestock, bread, grain, wine, and other estate resources without payment, while refusing to leave until Penelope chooses a husband. They mock Telemachus, mistreat strangers, drag the women servants about, force them to lie with them, and dishonor Penelope. Their conduct leaves the household without Ulysses’s protection and provokes Telemachus’s grievance and intended public confrontation. Ulysses later warns that their wasting of his estate and dishonor of his wife will end in bloodshed upon his return. In the end, he directly accuses them, and Eurymachus admits their great wrong.
Mentes, son of Anchialus and chief of the Taphians, is Ulysses’ friend and visits Ithaca trading; Minerva assumes this identity, and Telemachus later tells the suitors the visitor was a goddess.

Euryclea is an aged, trusted nurse and household servant connected to Ulysses, Telemachus, and Penelope. Daughter of Ops, she received and nursed Ulysses from birth, nurses Telemachus, serves as Penelope’s old nurse, and acts as Ulysses’ faithful housekeeper, responsible for stores and set over the household women. She knows the women’s conduct and keeps Telemachus’s voyage secret from Penelope. In Book XIX, she shuts the women in their room at Telemachus’s request, then washes a stranger’s feet at Penelope’s command. His figure, voice, and feet remind her of Ulysses; touching the scar from his wild-boar hunt confirms his identity. Though she privately identifies him, Ulysses requires silence, and she loyally keeps it. In Book XXII, she reports that fifty women are in the house and identifies twelve who have misconducted themselves, summons women, and brings fire and sulphur as commanded. In Book XXIII, she joyfully tells Penelope that Ulysses has returned and killed the suitors, helps prepare the bedchamber, and urges Ulysses to wear clean clothes.

Laertes is Ulysses’ aged father, a former ruler of the Cephallenians who lives sorrowfully on the country farm and house he reclaimed through labor. Distressed by Ulysses’ absence and his wife’s death, he prays to die peacefully at home. Ulysses recognizes and reunites with him through a scar and knowledge of the vineyard; despite old age, Laertes joins Ulysses in the Ithacan civil conflict and kills Eupeithes.

Antinous is Eupeithes’s son, a foremost youth of Ithaca, and the leading spokesman and ringleader among Penelope’s suitors. He is portrayed as insolent, wicked, bitter-tongued, and abusive toward Ulysses’s household, especially its servants. He blames Penelope for delaying remarriage through her weaving trick, mocks Telemachus’s planned voyage, and grows furious when Telemachus sails. As leader of the suitors, he orders a ship and chooses twenty men to ambush and kill Telemachus, also urging that Telemachus be seized before he can appeal to the assembly so that Ulysses’s property can be divided. At the house, he mistreats Eumaeus and the disguised Ulysses, refusing the stranger food and striking him with a footstool. He oversees the suitors’ contests, including the fight with Irus and attempts to make the bow usable. His actions culminate when Ulysses kills him first among the suitors, shooting him through the throat as he raises a cup. Eurymachus calls him the chief offender, saying he sought Telemachus’s death and foremost power in Ithaca.

Eurymachus, son of Polybus, is a leading suitor of Penelope and ringleader among the suitors: an understanding man who dismisses bird omens and has an improper relationship with Melantho. He deceptively claims friendship with Telemachus while plotting against him, proposes pursuing his ship, falsely reassures Penelope, praises and gifts her, then mocks the disguised Ulysses and violently throws a footstool.

Nestor, son of Neleus, rules Pylos and has reigned for three generations as guardian of the public weal. Husband of Eurydice and father of several sons, including Pisistratus, he is known for counsel and generous hospitality. When Telemachus and Minerva arrive during a Pylian sacrifice, Nestor receives them, recounts the Achaeans’ troubled return and deaths, advises a visit to Menelaus, recognizes Minerva, sacrifices to her, and sends Telemachus onward with horses, provisions, and Pisistratus.

Menelaus, son of Atreus and brother of Agamemnon, is a king who rules Argos and lives in Lacedaemon with Helen, his wife. He has a son, Megapenthes, and a daughter, Hermione, and possesses great riches gained through travel. After Troy, he urges an immediate return but is delayed by his steersman’s death, storms, wrecked ships, and a stay in Egypt, where he gathers treasure. Detained there, he captures Proteus and learns the fates of Achaeans, especially grieving for Odysseus. In Lacedaemon he generously hosts Telemachus and Pisistratus, hears of the suitors, recounts Troy and his return, and reports what he learned of Ulysses. He sends Telemachus home with hospitality and a silver-and-gold mixing bowl. After death, he is destined for the Elysian plain.
Eupeithes, father of Antinous, grieves his son's death, urges Ithacans to avenge the suitors, leads their armed attack on Ulysses, and is killed by Laertes in the Ithacan civil conflict.

Ulysses’ house is a large, fortified, well-built household with successive buildings, battlemented walls, strong double doors, cloisters, stores, arms, servants, and property. During Ulysses’ absence, the suitors occupy it, pursue Penelope, feast and make music there, consume its provisions without payment, mistreat its household and guests, and disgrace and waste the estate. Telemachus repeatedly asserts that it is his own house rather than a public house, prepares to leave secretly, and warns the suitors of punishment. Minerva visits it and makes the suitors drowsy; Penelope prays there for Telemachus. As Ulysses returns disguised as a beggar, he sees its scale and its corruption. He and Telemachus plan to remove and hide its armour, confront the suitors there, and kill them. In the end, the suitors’ bodies remain in the house uncared for, while their friends still do not know what happened.

l: the missing of Ulysses, The Odyssey
s: Ulysses’ disappearance has left no trace, and Telemachus does not know whether he is dead, lost at sea, or being detained by strangers. The uncertainty has brought grief to Telemachus and allowed the suitors to consume his property.

Telemachus’s voyage is a ship journey from Ithaca to Pylos and then Sparta, undertaken to learn whether Ulysses is alive, where he is, or how he died. Urged by Minerva, Telemachus secretly obtains provisions, a ship, and twenty men. With Minerva and his crew he reaches Pylos, questions Nestor, and is directed to continue to Lacedaemon to question Menelaus; if Ulysses is dead, he will return for funeral rites.

The assembly is a public council of Ithaca, convened after Ulysses’s departure and called by Telemachus. Minerva directs Telemachus to accuse the suitors before the gods; speakers debate the matter, but the gathering ends without restraining the suitors.

l: the suitors’ courtship of Penelope, The Odyssey
s: The suitors’ courtship of Penelope is a three-year pursuit at Ulysses’ house. Claiming to seek marriage, chiefs from Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus, and Ithaca remain there, offer wedding presents, demand that Penelope marry, rule the household, and consume Ulysses’ estate. Penelope neither plainly refuses nor concludes the matter, sending encouraging messages while secretly meaning otherwise. The unwanted pressure leaves her broken-hearted and helps motivate Ulysses’ planned revenge.

The suitors' feast is a meal in Ulysses' house, made from his household's oxen and other provisions. They sacrifice sheep, goats, pigs, and a heifer, prepare and distribute meat, bread, and wine, and eat and drink abundantly. Servants bring portions, and Ulysses receives bread, meat, and eventually a share equal to the others. A bard's music accompanies the banquet; after eating, the suitors demand singing and dancing. Insults and ominous signs attend the feast, with an expectation of a coming deadly meal. By evening, they return to their separate homes.

l: the prophecy of Ulysses’ return, The Odyssey
s: Minerva, speaking as Mentes, says that Ulysses is not dead and will probably return before long. She presents this as something borne in upon her from heaven rather than as a formal prophecy.

The ship belongs to Telemachus and serves his voyage with a crew of twenty men, first for travel to Pylos and then in search of Ulysses. Mentes says it lies in the harbour Rheithron beneath Neritum, while Minerva advises Telemachus to obtain a ship and later obtains one from Noemon son of Phronius. After sunset she brings it into the water, equips it with usual tackle, and stations it at the harbour’s end. It waits at Pylos with the crew and Menelaus’s gifts aboard; Minerva sends a favorable wind, and it sails toward Ithaca. It carries the crew, armour, and presents from Pylos to Ithaca, reaches Ithaca, is drawn onto land, and is unloaded after Telemachus remains in the country.

Minerva instructs Telemachus to summon the Achaean heroes to an assembly the next morning and publicly demand that the suitors leave. Telemachus repeats this plan when he tells the suitors to meet him in full assembly.

is_a friend of Ulysses [left in charge of Ulysses’s household] Mentor, described as a friend of Ulysses left in charge of his household and servants, condemns the people of Ithaca for allowing the suitors to abuse Ulysses's estate. He urges them to stop the wrongdoing, but Leiocritus rejects his appeal. Minerva later speaks to Telemachus in Mentor's likeness and voice.

The Ithacans assemble at Telemachus’s call, hear his complaint about the suitors, pity him, but disperse without acting. After the suitors’ deaths, they bury them and divide over vengeance: some heed Halitherses, while others follow Eupeithes into civil conflict until Minerva stops them.

l: the estate of Ulysses, The Odyssey
s: Ulysses's estate is a wealthy property with cattle, sheep, pigs, goats, wine, and other provisions. While Ulysses and then Telemachus are away, Penelope's suitors consume its resources without payment, depleting what it cannot sustain. Their threat escalates from wasteful feasting to a plan to kill Telemachus, divide the property, and take Penelope.

Telemachus’s crew is a ship’s company of twenty young men, about his own age, belonging to him and loyal out of friendship. Recruited as volunteers around Ithaca by Minerva, they accompany Telemachus in his search for Ulysses. They wait by the water, load stores, prepare the vessel, set its mast and sails, and depart. During a sacrifice, two guard the ship; later the crew again prepares, boards, and sails with Telemachus and Theoclymenus toward Ithaca.
Penelope's web is a burial pall for Laertes, woven by day and secretly unpicked by night for three years until maids reveal the deception and suitors force its completion.

Marriage to Penelope is a contested prospect shaped by the suitors, Telemachus, and Penelope’s delay. The suitors demand that she choose, while Penelope postpones remarriage by promising to finish Laertes’s burial pall. Telemachus refuses to send her to Icarius but says she may marry again if Ulysses is known dead. Antinous proposes separate offers, with the greatest offer winning her. Penelope ultimately declares that the man who strings Ulysses’s bow and shoots through twelve axes will marry her and receive her departure from her lawful husband’s house.

Ulysses's presumed death is the suitors' and Eumaeus's belief that he is long absent or dead, used to justify consuming his estate. Eurymachus places his death in a far country; Eumaeus imagines beasts or fish destroying him. Telemachus remains uncertain and seeks news before funeral arrangements.

Minerva, grey-eyed daughter of Jove, takes Mentor’s guise, serves Alcinous, sends a west wind, marks Ulysses’s disc, then makes the suitors drowsy and leads Telemachus to a ship, receiving drink offerings.

l: the house of Ulysses, The Odyssey
s: The house of Ulysses is a palace with outer and inner courts, a banqueting-cloister, threshold, gatehouse, Penelope’s room, women’s apartments, and a store-room containing treasures, a bow, and a quiver. During Ulysses’s absence, the suitors occupy it as a household and banquet residence, consuming its livestock, grain, wine, and estate and dishonouring it. Ulysses, disguised as a beggar, moves through the house; its doorway and court host the beggars’ quarrel and fight. Penelope brings out the bow for a contest to determine who will marry her and leave with her. As conflict nears, doors and gates are secured. After Ulysses kills the suitors, their corpses are piled in the gatehouse, and fire and sulphur purify the house before he prepares to leave temporarily while Penelope remains inside.
At Ulysses’ house, a crewed ship is loaded with stores and fitted with mast and white sails; a fair wind from the West sends it through deep blue water until dawn.
Minerva causes the suitors’ deep slumber by fuddling their drink; their eyes grow heavy, they drop their cups, and go to town to sleep.
Ulysses proposes going around the city to beg for drink and bread and to visit Ulysses’ house and the suitors. Telemachus tells the crew to take the ship on to the city while he goes to the herdsmen.

Pisistratus, Nestor’s only remaining unmarried son, serves as Telemachus’s companion and escort on his journey to Lacedaemon. He helps prepare a heifer for sacrifice, travels and sleeps alongside Telemachus, explains his plight to Menelaus, and recalls grief for Antilochus. He later helps Telemachus depart, drives him to Pylos, leaves him at his ship, and returns to report to Nestor.

Achilles is an Achaean hero, son of Peleus, prince, and foremost Achaean champion, fallen at Troy. After death he becomes a ghost among the dead in the meadow of asphodel, buried with Patroclus and Antilochus and honoured by Thetis. Meeting Ulysses, he values earthly life over rule among the dead, asks after Neoptolemus and Peleus, and laments his early death to Agamemnon.
Agamemnon’s wife, Clytemnestra helps murder him and kills Cassandra beside him, then is condemned by Agamemnon as cruel and shameless.

contains Cnossus [a great town] Crete is presented as the birthplace of the disguised stranger and the home of his father Castor son of Hylax. The stranger claims to have commanded Cretan men and ships and to have sailed from Crete on the raid against Egypt.

Lacedaemon, a low-lying city containing Sparta, is the destination of Telemachus’s long sea voyage with Pisistratus. They arrive and stay at Menelaus’s palace while Telemachus asks about Ulysses. Minerva comes there to fetch him, and, urged to return home, he leaves with Pisistratus.

Egypt is a place with the island Pharos off its coast. It is raided by Ulysses and his fleet and later targeted by a Cretan stranger, whose men ravage its land but are defeated. Menelaus is detained there until sacrifices, including holy hecatombs at its heaven-fed stream, permit his voyage to continue.

The sack of Troy, caused by Achaean warfare and stratagems, occurs in the war’s tenth year after nine years of effort. After the city is sacked, the Achaeans divide into groups and sail home, dispersed by heaven, beginning difficult homeward voyages.

The Achaean homeward voyage is disrupted by divine displeasure, quarrels, storms, deaths, and shipwrecks. Nestor sails with Diomed’s group toward Pylos, while Menelaus is driven toward Crete and Egypt and other leaders follow different routes.

l: quarrel between the sons of Atreus, The Odyssey
s: A quarrel between Agamemnon and Menelaus over the Achaean homeward voyage: after Troy falls, Menelaus urges immediate sailing, Agamemnon demands sacrifices first, dividing the Achaeans.

avenges Agamemnon [by killing Aegisthus] Orestes’s vengeance consists of returning from Athens and killing Aegisthus, who murdered Agamemnon. His act is praised as a noble vengeance that will preserve his name through time.
The chariot, provided by Nestor and drawn by fleet horses, carries Telemachus with Pisistratus driving from Pylos through Pherae toward Lacedaemon.
Nestor provides his best and fleetest horses for Telemachus’s journey; yoked to a chariot, they swiftly carry Telemachus and Pisistratus from Pylos toward Lacedaemon.

Hades is a dark, inaccessible house and realm of the dead, not reachable directly by ship. Ulysses must visit it before returning home, near the meeting of Pyriphlegethon, Cocytus, and Acheron. There he encounters ghosts, including Elpenor, who seeks burial rites, and the dead around Minos, punished figures, and the phantom of Hercules. Later, ghosts reach its dark abode after passing Oceanus, the rock Leucas, the gates of the sun, and the land of dreams.

provides hospitality [to Telemachus] Nestor’s house provides lodging for Telemachus, who sleeps there with Pisistratus. The household prepares the sacrifice, receives the guests for a meal, and supplies provisions for Telemachus’s journey.
A broad-browed, unbroken year-old heifer for Minerva, never yoked; its gilded horns precede its killing, cutting up, and offering in sacrifice.
A propitiatory offering to Minerva begins with Nestor's promise after her eagle appearance, then uses a gilded-horned heifer in prayers, offerings, burning, roasting, and eating.

l: Telemachus's journey to Pylos and Lacedaemon, The Odyssey
s: Telemachus’s journey is a secret voyage from Ithaca to Pylos and Lacedaemon to seek news of Ulysses. With a picked crew, he first visits Nestor at Pylos, who welcomes him but knows nothing. Nestor then sends him with Pisistratus by chariot toward Lacedaemon; after a night at Pherae, they reach Menelaus during a wedding feast. Menelaus and Helen speak with them about Ulysses, and Menelaus reports that the old man of the sea saw him grieving in Calypso’s house, unable to return. The suitors plot to murder Telemachus at sea, but he reaches Ithaca safely before they can intercept him.

The ritual includes cutting the victims’ tongues, making drink-offerings, washing hands, sprinkling barley meal, praying, burning offerings, and sharing the cooked meat. Nestor performs these acts with his sons, household, Telemachus’s crew, and Minerva’s favor.

Hospitality is protected by Jove and shown as a duty toward strangers and suppliants. Alcinous lavishly receives Ulysses with gifts, care, food, entertainment, and safe packing for departure. Eumaeus likewise aids the disguised Ulysses despite doubting him. In contrast, Polyphemus rejects hospitality and Zeus’s protection, refusing mercy and eating his visitors.

Helen, Menelaus’s lawful wife and Hermione’s mother, recognizes Odysseus and Telemachus’s resemblance to him. In recounting Odysseus’s disguised entry into Troy, she uses a sorrow-banishing Egyptian herb from Polydamna to comfort guests, then prepares their beds.

l: the voyage from Troy, The Odyssey
s: The voyage from Troy is a hazardous return marked by divine demands, delays, storms, and uncertain homecoming. Menelaus is held by gods and wind near Pharos, learns from Proteus to sacrifice in Egypt, then gains a fair wind and returns after nearly eight years through many lands. Ulysses’s party reaches Ismarus, is driven past Cape Malea and Cythera for nine days, and arrives among the Lotus-eaters; his return remains unfinished under Calypso.

l: Odysseus’s disguise in Troy, The Odyssey
s: Odysseus covered himself with wounds and bruises, dressed in rags, and entered Troy looking like a menial or beggar. Helen recognized him, questioned him, washed and anointed him, gave him clothes, and kept his mission secret until he returned safely to the Greek camp.

The wooden horse, made by Epeus with Minerva’s assistance, conceals the bravest Argives and Achaeans, including Ulysses. While they wait inside, Odysseus prevents Anticlus from answering Helen’s imitated voices. The Trojans draw the horse into their fortress as an offering, enabling the hidden warriors to attack and destroy the city.

contains wedding gifts and treasures [described as splendid and richly furnished] Menelaus’s palace is richly furnished with bronze, gold, amber, ivory, and silver. Telemachus and Pisistratus are bathed, clothed, fed, and given beds there while Menelaus and Helen receive them as honored guests.
Menelaus’s household welcomes Telemachus and Pisistratus, tending their horses, bathing and clothing them, feeding them, and providing sleep amid a wedding feast with music and tumblers.

l: grief for the dead and missing, The Odyssey
s: Grief over Odysseus’s absence and Troy’s dead afflicts Penelope and Menelaus, expands into shared remembrance and weeping with Pisistratus and Telemachus, then Helen eases it.
Idothea is a goddess and daughter of Proteus who pities stranded Menelaus at Pharos, prepares an ambush with seal skins and ambrosia, and enables him to capture Proteus.

Proteus is an old immortal Egyptian of the sea who serves Neptune, knows its depths and distant events, and changes into many forms. Menelaus and three companions seize him among his seals and withstand his transformations until he resumes his true form, then he reveals how Menelaus may finish his voyage and the Achaeans’ fates.
Pharos is an island near Egypt with a good harbour; Menelaus is becalmed there for twenty days until Idothea helps him reach the open sea.

l: the capture of Proteus, The Odyssey
s: requires ambush [with three men concealed under seal skins] Menelaus and three trusted men hide in pits beneath seal skins and wait for Proteus to finish counting his seals and fall asleep. They seize him, maintain their grip through his transformations, and force him to reveal the gods’ demands and the fates of the Achaeans.

l: the women of the household, The Odyssey
s: The women are female servants and household maids in Ulysses’ house. Some secretly sleep with the suitors and are said by Telemachus to be insolent to him and Penelope. They remove bodies and clean, are confined and hanged, while surviving women return with torches to embrace Ulysses.

l: the suitors' plot to kill Telemachus, The Odyssey
s: This is the suitors' unsuccessful plot to murder Telemachus before he returns home, driven by their fear of the trouble he may cause. Led by Antinous with twenty men, they sail to wait in the straits between Ithaca and Samos. Minerva doubts their success. Telemachus returns before they can capture him, and they consider attacking him at his farm or on the road. Penelope learns of the plan through Medon and rebukes Antinous. An eagle omen leads Amphinomus to predict failure and send them to dinner.
Penelope’s dream is a vision sent by Minerva resembling Iphthime, comforting Penelope with Telemachus’s promised return but refusing to reveal whether Ulysses lives or dies.
The suitors establish an ambush at Asteris between Ithaca and Samos, waiting with a ship to murder Telemachus during his return voyage.

is_threatened_by the suitors’ plot to murder Telemachus [during his return from Pylos and Lacedaemon] Telemachus’s safety is threatened by the suitors, who plan to kill him at sea before he reaches home. Minerva’s message gives Penelope hope that he will return, but the outcome is not yet known.
Ino, also called Leucothea, is a former mortal turned marine goddess who pities Ulysses, gives him her enchanted protective veil and advice, then receives the scarf back from the river.

The Phaeacians are a people of Scheria, living apart from other people at the sea’s end. Near of kin to the gods and blessed with abundance, they are ruled by Alcinous and are renowned as the world’s best seafarers, proud of their ships, masts, and oars. They also excel in running, other athletic contests, dancing, and appreciation of Demodocus’ songs. Though described as disliking strangers, they hold that strangers in distress are protected by Jove and become conspicuous hosts to Ulysses. They had formerly lived near the lawless Cyclopes, who plundered them, until Nausithous moved them to Scheria. When Ulysses arrives, their leaders make offerings and agree to send him home. At Alcinous’ summons they gather, feast, compete, dance, hear Ulysses’ account, and supply him with cloaks, shirts, gold, and other valuable gifts. Their ships need neither pilots nor rudders and know cities and countries throughout the world.
