Finally, they carry the sleeping Ulysses safely from Scheria to Ithaca; on the return, Neptune turns their ship to stone, leaving them afraid that their city may be buried under a mountain.
return_from Troy The Argive Danaans are described as returning from Troy and suffering misfortunes arranged by the gods so that future generations would have stories to sing about.

Scheria is the fertile, inhabited land and home of the Phaeacians, settled far from other people. It contains a walled town or city with houses, temples, divided lands, harbours, and seafaring associations. Assigned by Jove and aided by Minerva as Ulysses’s safe destination after his perilous voyage, it first appears to him as mountainous, rocky, spray-covered coast without an evident safe harbour. After his raft is wrecked, he reaches Scheria and is guided to the palace. Its Phaeacians escort him to Ithaca with gifts; afterward Neptune turns their returning ship to stone and threatens the city with burial under a mountain.
Ulysses builds a seaworthy timber raft with steering and sail, sent by Calypso; after departure, Neptune’s storm destroys it, leaving Ulysses briefly using a plank before swimming away.

protects Ulysses [while worn around his chest] Ino’s veil is enchanted and protects Ulysses from harm while he wears it. Ino tells him to remove it when he reaches land and throw it back into the sea.

l: Ulysses's voyage from Ogygia, The Odyssey
s: Ulysses’s twenty-day voyage from Ogygia begins when Calypso sends him away on a provisioned raft with clothing and a favorable wind. Near Scheria, after sighting the Phaeacian coast, Neptune raises a storm that destroys the raft. Ulysses swims ashore, reaches a river, and sleeps among leaves until Nausicaa finds him.
Neptune’s storm gathers clouds and winds, raises a tremendous sea, throws Ulysses overboard, breaks the mast, and destroys the raft.

The sea causes Ulysses’s shipwreck and twenty-day wandering, carrying him from the Ogygian island toward the Phaeacian coast. It holds him beneath a heavy swell, then calms, but its violent surf, deep water, and rocky coast nearly destroy him. It also surrounds the Phaeacians’ land, harbours, and seafaring.

A wave catches Ulysses and throws him against the rocks, where he clings to them until the water retreats. Another wave carries him back into the sea, tears the skin from his hands, and draws him underwater.

l: river (the river Ulysses reaches), The Odyssey
s: has river god (the god of the river Ulysses reaches) [as its governing deity] Ulysses finds the mouth of a river while swimming along the coast and chooses it because it has no rocks and shelters him from the wind. Its current carries him toward safety, and its waters become calm when the river god responds to Ulysses' prayer.

l: river god (the god of the river Ulysses reaches), The Odyssey
s: A god of the river Ulysses reaches, he hears Ulysses’ prayer, stills the stream and waves, and safely brings Ulysses into the river’s mouth.

shelter Ulysses [from the cold and weather] The woods on high ground provide Ulysses with shelter from the cold and damp. Beneath two closely growing olive shoots, he makes a bed from dead leaves and sleeps safely.
Teiresias says that Ulysses’s death will come from the sea when he is full of years and peace of mind. His life will ebb away gently, and his people will bless him.

Nausicaa is a lovely Phaeacian princess, daughter of Alcinous, protected by Minerva and admired by the best young men among her people. Following Minerva’s instruction, she travels with her maids by waggon to wash clothes. When Ulysses approaches, she stands firm rather than fleeing, gives him clothes, oil, food, and aid, and directs him to her father’s house, saving him from danger. Though worried that Phaeacians will gossip if she is seen with him, she returns home with her brothers. Ulysses credits her rescue, defends her before Alcinous, and calls her his guardian angel; she admires him and asks not to be forgotten.

Alcinous is king of the Phaeacians, holding the whole power of their state after Nausithous’s death. Husband of Arete and father of Nausicaa, he lives in the town’s finest house and first appears providing Nausicaa with a waggon and mules. His central importance is as a powerful, generous host and organizer of Ulysses’s return. He receives Ulysses from the hearth, seats and feeds him, orders offerings and a bed, and promises either escort home or, should he remain, a house, estate, and marriage to Nausicaa. He leads the Phaeacians in assembly, has a new ship manned, hosts a banquet, and responds to Ulysses’s distress by redirecting the gathering toward sports and dance. He praises Phaeacian skill, requires gifts of clothing and gold for Ulysses, makes Euryalus apologize and give a present, arranges a bath, and adds a golden goblet. Recognizing Ulysses as well disposed rather than deceptive, he asks for his account of those who went to Troy and died, while repeatedly assuring him of gifts and escort. At the end, he adds tripods and cauldrons, secures the gifts aboard ship, sends Ulysses away, and recognizes Neptune’s punishment as fulfillment of an old prophecy.
Nausicaa’s household servants accompany her to wash and fold clothes and play ball, flee Ulysses, then return at her command with aid.

Phaeacian city is a walled coastal place with two narrow-entranced harbours, roadside ships, assemblies, a market, Neptune’s temple, and Alcinous’s palace. Its people make and use ship’s gear. Ulysses crosses it unseen under Minerva’s concealment; later, Neptune threatens to bury it beneath a high mountain.

belongs_to Alcinous [his excellent father’s house] Alcinous’s royal house has gates, an outer court, and an inner court. Nausicaa directs Ulysses to find her mother spinning purple wool by the fire and to appeal to her by clasping her knees, while Alcinous sits nearby.
A strong waggon, drawn by mules, carries Nausicaa, her maids, and clothes to the washing cisterns, then returns folded clothes toward town.

feed_on herbage [by the water side] The mules are harnessed to Nausicaa’s waggon and carry it to the water side. They feed by the washing cisterns and later draw the waggon steadily toward the town and Minerva’s sacred grove.

are_washed_at washing cisterns [with pure water sufficient for any quantity of linen] Nausicaa’s clothes are initially lying in disorder, prompting Minerva’s advice about a washing day. The clothes are washed, dried, folded, placed in the waggon, and some are given to Ulysses after his shipwreck.

contain pure water [available at all times] The washing cisterns lie some distance from the town and have a constant supply of pure water. Nausicaa and her maids use them to wash the clothes before laying them by the sea to dry.

is_a sacred grove [dedicated to Minerva] Minerva’s sacred grove contains poplars, a well, and a meadow, and lies near the road to the town. Nausicaa directs Ulysses to wait there, and he later prays there for a hospitable reception.

Phaeacian ships are pilotless, rudderless vessels that understand Phaeacian thoughts and wishes. They know cities and countries throughout the world and glide across the sea like thought or a bird, even through mist and cloud. Alcinous promises they will carry Ulysses wherever he wishes and travel beyond Euboea in a day, though they are said to risk wreck when returning from an escort.

Minerva proposes a washing day so Nausicaa can clean the household clothes and prepare good linen for her family and attendants. Nausicaa presents the request to Alcinous by mentioning the clothes needed for him and her brothers.

l: meeting between Nausicaa and Ulysses, The Odyssey
s: Nausicaa meets Ulysses after the ball game wakes him from his sleep among the leaves. She listens to his appeal, recognizes him as sensible and well-disposed, and helps him with clothing, food, washing, and directions to the royal house.

l: Ulysses's shipwreck and wanderings, The Odyssey
s: begins_at Ogygian island [from which the winds and waves carried Ulysses] Ulysses has been struggling at sea for twenty days, carried from the Ogygian island by winds and waves. He reaches the Phaeacian coast exhausted, naked, and covered with salt water, fearing that further suffering may still await him.

Phaeacian hospitality is a custom toward strangers and foreigners in distress, who are under Jove’s protection. It begins with kindness, food, drink, clothes, washing, and guidance, then provides a feast, music, dancing, sports, clean linen, warm baths, good beds, and a ship, crew, and escort.
Marriage is Nausicaa’s anticipated future, prompted by Minerva’s advice to prepare clothes; though she avoids naming it to Alcinous, Ulysses praises harmonious spouses as creating a peaceful home.

Arete is the greatly respected queen and wife of Alcinous among the Phaeacians, valued for goodness, judgment, and influence. When Ulysses arrives as her guest, she recognizes clothes made by her and her maids, questions his identity and journey, and orders a bed prepared for him.

l: palace of King Alcinous, The Odyssey
s: King Alcinous’s palace is a richly adorned, guarded residence with bronze, gold, and silver features, servants, and a fertile garden. Ulysses enters under Minerva’s darkness and supplicates Arete and Alcinous.

Odyssey homeward voyage is Ulysses’s Phaeacian escort home. Alcinous promises safe passage, and the Phaeacians prepare gifts, festivities, and a ship despite Neptune’s anger at their readiness to escort travelers. In one night, they carry the sleeping Ulysses from Scheria to Ithaca; they return home, and Neptune punishes their ship for helping him.
Alcinous plans a magnificent banquet in honour of Ulysses; guests eat and drink, Demodocus sings as Ulysses hides tears, then athletic games follow.

protects suppliants [under Jove's protection] The Phaeacians treat Ulysses as a suppliant under the protection of Jove. Alcinous removes him from the ashes of the hearth, gives him food and drink, and promises assistance, while the household prepares a bed for him.

uses Phaeacian ships [swift and capable of long voyages] The Phaeacians are described as the best sailors in the world, and their ships are said to travel with extraordinary speed and ease. Their maritime skill is presented as superior to that of all other peoples.

A new Phaeacian ship, manned by fifty-two sailors, is fitted and launched to escort Ulysses home. It swiftly carries him asleep from Scheria to Ithaca and reaches the harbour of Phorcys. Returning, it is transformed by Neptune into stone and rooted in the ground near Scheria.

Demodocus is a blind, Muse-beloved bard, inspired by heaven and favored and honored by others. At a banquet he is seated, fed, given wine and his lyre, and sings of Ulysses and Achilles’ quarrel. During athletic games he sings of Mars, Venus, and Vulcan. Later, after receiving roast pork from Ulysses, he accurately sings of the wooden horse, Troy’s sack, and Ulysses’s fighting. His song moves a guest to groan and lament, so he is asked to stop.

include athletic contests [boxing, wrestling, jumping, running, and disc throwing] The athletic games follow the banquet and include foot races, wrestling, jumping, discus throwing, and boxing. Clytoneus wins the race, Euryalus wrestling, Amphialus jumping, Elatreus discus throwing, and Laodamas boxing until Ulysses outthrows the Phaeacians with a heavier discus.
Euryalus, a Phaeacian athlete resembling Mars, excels at wrestling but rudely insults Ulysses; after Ulysses rebukes him, he apologizes and gives him a sword.

include disc [among the competitions] The athletic contests are presented as a way for the Phaeacians to display their superiority as boxers, wrestlers, jumpers, and runners. Ulysses initially declines to compete because of his troubles, but Euryalus’ taunt leads him to enter the discus contest and surpass every Phaeacian mark.

Circe is a great, cunning Aeaean goddess and enchantress, child of the sun by Perse, sister of Mercury and Aeetes, who lives on Aeaean island in her own house with four maid servants. She practices magic with drugs and a wand, transforms people, and weaves an exceptionally fine web. She drugs Ulysses’s men and turns them into pigs, then restores them and gives the company food, clothing, washing, shelter, and time to recover. She becomes an adviser and helper to Ulysses: she teaches him to fasten a bond, directs him to visit Hades and Proserpine’s house, supplies sacrificial animals, and sends the crew onward with a fair wind. After their return, she feeds them and explains the voyage ahead, warning of the Sirens, Wanderers, Scylla, Charybdis, and especially the sun-god’s island, where the crew faces its worst danger.

Ulysses’ treasure is a collection of Phaeacian gifts: bronze, gold, clothing, tripods, cauldrons, cloaks, shirts, a sword, and a golden goblet. Arete packs gifts in a chest, which Ulysses fastens. After waking, he counts everything, finds nothing missing, and stores it with Minerva in the Cave of the Naiads.

l: song of the Trojan horse, The Odyssey
s: A song by Demodocus describes the wooden horse and Troy’s sack. It tells of Achaeans sailing away or hiding inside the horse, Trojans bringing it into their fortress, and Achaeans emerging to destroy Troy, including Ulysses and Menelaus fighting at Deiphobus’s house; it makes the guest lament.
Laodamas and Halius perform alone with Polybus's red ball, throwing and catching it while dancing as young men applaud and stamp their feet.

is_caused_by song of the Trojan horse [on hearing Demodocus sing] Ulysses weeps when Demodocus sings about the wooden horse and the destruction of Troy. He cries as painfully as a woman grieving over a husband killed defending his city, but only Alcinous notices his tears, sobs, and sighs.
The guest's travels are not described; he is asked to recount where he wandered, the countries, peoples, and cities he encountered, and which were hostile, uncivilised, hospitable, or humane.

is_a people The Cicons are the people of Ismarus and its surrounding region. After Ulysses' men raid the city, inland Cicons come to its aid; they are more numerous, stronger, and skilled in fighting from chariots or on foot, and they defeat Ulysses' forces.
City of the Cicons, sacked by Ulysses and his men after Troy; they kill inhabitants, take wives and booty, then depart after a counterattack.

Odysseus’s twelve ships carry Ulysses and his men from Troy. A hurricane tears their sails, but after shelter and repair they sail again and escape the Lotus-eaters. They later beach on a wooded, fertile island; Odysseus’s ship carries twelve companions into Polyphemus’s country while the others remain nearby.
The Lotus-eaters are people who live on lotus and offer it to visitors; it causes Ulysses' scouts to forget home and want to stay.

causes forgetfulness of home [in those who eat it] The lotus is a delicious food that causes those who eat it to stop caring about home and to forget their return. Ulysses' men who taste it must be forced back to the ships.

l: the land of the Lotus-eaters, The Odyssey
s: is_a land [inhabited by the Lotus-eaters] The lotus-eaters' land is reached on the tenth day after Ulysses is driven across the sea by foul winds. Ulysses and his crew land there to obtain fresh water and eat a midday meal before he sends scouts to investigate the inhabitants.

l: the raid on Ismarus, The Odyssey
s: is_a raid [conducted by Ulysses and his men] The raid on Ismarus involves Ulysses and his men sacking the city, killing its people, taking wives and booty, and dividing the spoils fairly. Ulysses urges an immediate departure, but his men delay until the Cicons gather against them.

l: the battle with the Cicons, The Odyssey
s: is_a battle [between Ulysses's forces and the Cicons] The battle with the Cicons begins after the inland Cicons come to aid the people of Ismarus. Ulysses' men hold their own through the morning, but the Cicons gain the advantage as the day ends, killing six men from every ship.

is_a food [delicious and made from a kind of flower] The Lotus-eaters' lotus is so pleasurable that Ulysses' scouts no longer care about home or returning to report what they have learned. Ulysses restrains the affected men under the ship benches and warns the rest not to taste it.

l: the land of the Cyclopes, The Odyssey
s: is_inhabited_by Cyclopes The land of the Cyclopes is inhabited by people described as lawless and inhuman. Its inhabitants live in caves on high mountains, while the surrounding country has wild crops, sheep, goats, and stubble fires.
